Brains model the world in a handful of simplified dimensions. States in those dimensions drive action back out into the world, and the consequences of that action hold the model to account.

Hello! I'm a systems neuroscience researcher at the Medical University of Vienna, working with the labs of Sanja Bauer Mikulovic and Balázs Hangya. I study how the brain builds usable representations of the world, combining in-vivo electrophysiology and imaging, machine learning and computational modelling, in both healthy mice and mouse models of disease.

## How I think about the brain

<!--
  SKELETON - the paragraphs below are a placeholder in your voice, meant to be

  5. What would change your mind.

The unit I care about is the population, not the cell. A brain area earns its
keep not by responding to something but by holding a structure that downstream
circuits can read and act on, which is why questions about geometry — what shape
a representation has, how much it can distinguish, whether it transfers to a new
environment — interest me more than questions about what any individual neuron
prefers.

A second commitment follows from the first: a representation is only as useful
as its binding to the world. A code can be perfectly formed and still be wrong
about where the animal is. Much of what I find worth chasing sits in that gap,
and I write about it in more detail under [ideas]({{ '/ideas/' | relative_url }}).

## How I got here

I completed my PhD at the University of Edinburgh in 2023, funded by the Medical
Research Council Precision Medicine programme, and stayed on as a postdoctoral
researcher in Matt Nolan's lab. That work asked when grid cell firing actually
contributes to behaviour, and found that it matters specifically when an animal
has to path integrate rather than follow a cue.

I have since moved to the Medical University of Vienna, working with the Sanja
Bauer Mikulovic and Balázs Hangya labs.
